extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers and historians of science; practitioners interested in early scientific method and observational practice
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for conducting seventeenth-century natural philosophy: preparing the mind, collecting and recording observations, using instruments and cross-validation, and specific requirements for meteorological observation (Hooke's method).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation — prepare the mind and furnish it with fit materials
rubrics_metrics.description: "containing the manner of preparing the mind, and furnishing it with fit materials to work on"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First part only of Hooke's 'Algebra of Discovery' was written; this 'Preparation' includes classification of errors incidental to humanity and is a patient, practical process. Preparation is prerequisite to attempting to raise new axioms or theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use skillfully constructed instruments to help the senses
rubrics_metrics.description: "The senses are to be helped ... by skillfully constructed instruments, whereby their sphere of action may be enlarged, and their untutored impressions brought to the test of exact measurement and rigid calculation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruments enlarge sensory reach and allow exact measurement and rigid calculation; invention and improvement of instruments are central to reliable observation (examples in the text: telescopes, micrometers, barometers, hygrometers, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-validate sensory reports until sensation is standardized
rubrics_metrics.description: "The report of one sense must be corrected by comparison with that of the others, until 'sensation is reduced to a standard,' and the mind is gradually informed with true notions of 'things, as they are ... not only as they have this or that peculiar relation or influence on our own senses or selves.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare independent sense-reports; reduce subjective impressions to objective, standardized measures through corroboration across modalities and instruments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compile a 'Philosophical History' — assembled, ordered repository of observations
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'brief and plain account of a great store of choice and significant natural and artificial operations, actions, and effects, ranged in a convenient order, and interwoven ... with some short hints of accidental remarks or theories, of corresponding or disagreeing received opinions, of doubts and queryies, and the like.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect and arrange facts and notable operations in a convenient order, with occasional notes on theories, disagreements, doubts and queries. The repository must be well stocked before attempting to raise new axioms or theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope — include the whole 'matter of the world' in the history
rubrics_metrics.description: "The matter of such a history ... is no less than the world; for there is no body or operation in the universe that is not some way or other to be taken notice of in this great work."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The envisioned scope is encyclopedic: include phenomena from ether to anthracite, from stars to quotidian crafts. Nothing is to be excluded; both artisanal and scientific practices are valuable sources of facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be 'knowing in hypotheses' and technically skilled
rubrics_metrics.description: The natural historian was to be 'knowing in hypotheses,' a skilled mechanician, and an able mathematician, "that he might investigate their relations by experiment, and deduce the consequences of such relations by calculation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine hypothesis-awareness with experimental skill and mathematical competence so that observed facts can be tested experimentally and their consequences derived quantitatively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postpone raising axioms until the repository is stocked
rubrics_metrics.description: "Until this repository be pretty well stored with choice and sound materials, the work of raising new axioms or theories is not to be attempted, lest beginning without materials the whole design be given over in the middle."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize empirical accumulation and ordering of facts before attempting to formulate general laws; avoid premature theorizing without adequate data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'Helps of Discovery' (Prerogative Instances) in the preparatory stage
rubrics_metrics.description: Hooke's 'Helps of Discovery' are likened to Bacon's 'Prerogative Instances' but placed in the preparatory stage of inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ selected exemplars or particularly informative instances as preparatory tools to guide observation and hypothesis formation prior to formal generalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formulate explicit queries to direct investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Hooke provided concrete questions under headings such as 'Ether' and 'Of the atmosphere' (e.g., Whether ether permeates all bodies? Whether it causes gravity? Whether each planet has a peculiar atmosphere? Whether sunspots may be clouds?).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct empirical inquiry by posing clear, specific questions about phenomena; the article reproduces many such queries as exemplars to guide future investigators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meteorological observation — record strength and quarter of the winds
rubrics_metrics.description: Listed as item 1 in Hooke's 'Method for making a History of the Weather': 'The strength and quarter of the winds.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wind direction and force must be systematically observed and recorded as requisite particulars for deriving laws of weather.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meteorological observation — record degrees of heat and cold
rubrics_metrics.description: Listed as item 2 in Hooke's requisites: 'The degrees of heat and cold.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematic temperature measurements (degrees of heat/cold) are essential data for a history of the weather.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meteorological observation — record degrees of dryness and moisture (hygroscope)
rubrics_metrics.description: Listed as item 3: 'The degrees of dryness and moisture observed with a hygroscope "made with the single beard of a wild oat ... set upright and headed with an index."'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record atmospheric humidity using a hygroscope (Hooke suggests a simple botanical hygroscope) and index changes; include hygrometric observations as standard practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meteorological observation — record degrees of air pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: Listed as item 4: 'The degrees of pressure of the air.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Barometric (air pressure) data must be systematically collected as a core variable in weather histories and for deriving empirical rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meteorological observation — record the constitution and face of the sky
rubrics_metrics.description: Listed as item 5: 'The constitution and face of the sky.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Qualitative description of sky conditions (cloudiness, appearance, notable features) should accompany quantitative meteorological measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt a broad, discursive approach — collect varied observations and 'lucky hits'
rubrics_metrics.description: Hooke argues it is better 'to embrace the influences of Providence, and to be diligent in the inquiry of everything we meet with' and that 'the number of considerable observations and inventions this way collected will a hundredfold outstrip those that are found by design.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor wide-ranging, opportunistic observation over narrow, single-subject obsession; variety often yields more discoveries and is more engaging for author and reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat hypotheses as pragmatic classifiers with utilitarian aim
rubrics_metrics.description: Hooke's view (reflecting the Royal Society's aims): hypotheses are valuable when they 'provide a convenient classification of experiments' and when their application 'will improve and facilitate the present way of manual arts.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value hypotheses for plausibility and practical utility in organizing experiments and improving applications, while recognizing they are not necessarily ultimate truths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholarly conduct — acknowledge and integrate others' discoveries
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrative criticizes Hooke's intellectual egotism for rejecting Newton's findings; good practice implied is to acknowledge and integrate valid results from peers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be open to competitors' results and ready to incorporate them into one's work rather than dismissing them out of pride; correspondence and conciliatory exchange are encouraged.
